title: Income Gradients in Systolic Blood Pressure: Education Adjustment and Survey Using Weighted Regression in NHANES 2021-2023
content: Income and education capture distinct but interrelated dimensions of socioeconomic resources. This study examines the association between the family income-to-poverty ratio (PIR) and measured systolic blood pressure (SBP), comparing estimates before and after adjustment for body mass index (BMI) and education. Four NHANES components were linked, and eligibility, repeated measurements, pregnancy status and variable completeness were assessed to obtain a common sample of 5019 adults. Three linear models incorporated examination weights, strata and primary sampling units, sequentially adjusting for demographic characteristics, BMI and education. Each one-unit higher PIR was associated with an SBP difference of -0.682 mmHg after demographic adjustment (95% CI -1.193 to -0.171), -0.656 after adding BMI (-1.193 to -0.119), and -0.201 after adding education (-1.014 to 0.612). Education adjustment substantially attenuated the income gradient, whereas BMI adjustment changed it little. Presenting these models together shows how the interpretation of income-related blood pressure differences depends on the dimensions of social resources included in the comparison.
